1. Fixed drug eruption (most likely) — fits recurrent flares localized to the same mid/lower back site, histology showing interface dermatitis with dyskeratosis, eosinophilic spongiosis and pigment incontinence (dermal melanophages); DIF negative and fungal tests negative support this.

2. Eczematous dermatitis (nummular or allergic contact dermatitis) — eosinophilic spongiosis and neutrophilic exocytosis are typical of eczema; recurrent localized flares possible though failure to respond to potent topical/systemic steroids makes this less likely.

3. Lichen planus (lichenoid dermatitis) — interface dermatitis with dyskeratosis can be seen in LP; distribution and clinical morphology would help distinguish (violaceous papules, mucosal involvement).

4. Erythema dyschromicum perstans (ashy dermatosis) — chronic gray-brown macules on trunk with interface change and pigment incontinence can produce similar biopsy findings, though clinical color and chronicity differ.

5. Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus — interface dermatitis and dyskeratosis can occur; typically photodistributed and serologies/DIF may be variable — less likely given location and negative DIF.

Recommended next steps to confirm diagnosis and guide management:
- Obtain a focused, detailed medication/OTC/herbal/NSAID/antibiotic history to look for temporal correlation with flares (highest-yield step for fixed drug eruption).
- Correlate clinical morphology (photograph of an active lesion) and note whether lesions recur in precisely the same spot.
- Consider targeted provocation testing or patch testing for suspected causative drug only under controlled conditions if clinically necessary.
